proposed_en_title: Black Moon Lilith Calculator: Find Your Lilith Sign, Degree and House (Mean and True)

backend_calls.endpoint: POST https://astro-rapor.onrender.com/api/harita (lilith.js:7 and 95; handler server.js:745-829; geocode in lib/geo.js)
backend_calls.fields_shown_to_user: The page uses only fixed vocabulary from the response: gezegenler[].ad/burc/derece, yukselen.burc/derece, mc.burc/derece and evler[].ev/burc/derece. These go through hazirla() (lilith.js:99-106) and are turned into numeric longitudes and house cusps. Turkish planet names show up in two places: the aspect card headers (lilith.js:174, esc(x.a), e.g. 'Venüs · kavuşum') and the transit list ('Transit Lilith, natal ' + o.a, lilith.js:194). Sign names on screen come from the client arrays, not from the server. On failure, the server's Turkish j.mesaj or j.errors text is shown as-is in .li-msg (lilith.js:96, 237, 239). Not used or not shown: yorum (Turkish prose from noktaYorumu), not, cark (deleted at lilith.js:97), dogumBilgi, acilar, elementDengesi.
backend_calls.notes: Only called when both birth time and birth place are given (lilith.js:229). Without them, sign, degree, true Lilith, return dates and the 1930-2040 table are all computed in the browser. Because the page reads only fixed vocabulary, a client-side TR->EN dictionary (sign/planet names, as in lib/mcp-dil.js) is enough, and no backend change is needed. The EN JS must keep the Turkish BN array and the Turkish planet keys (PG/ACIK/TEMA/TRANSIT, N.p['Ay'] at lilith.js:110) for parsing, and translate only what is displayed. Three things to watch: (1) The 429 message is Turkish and says 'Dilersen Raporlar'a göz atabilirsin', a paid-report upsell (server.js:748-752). The EN page must ignore mesaj/errors and show its own English messages. (2) geocode() quietly falls back to Ankara when a place isn't found (lib/geo.js:5, 106-113), so a foreign user would get wrong houses with no warning. The client can check dogumBilgi.yer === 'Ankara (varsayılan)' and warn, or the backend could return ok:false. (3) Geocoding searches with language=tr, but worldwide lookup works (Open-Meteo, plus ULKE_KOD covers English country names). Rate limit is 60 calls per IP per day.

shared_scripts.needed_for_en: Yes, it is the whole tool (336 lines). It has about 170 Turkish user-facing strings: about 65 fixed-vocabulary items (BN signs, YE/DE suffix forms, months AYL, planet keys) and about 60 prose strings (TEMA, EVAD house names, TRANSIT texts, opposition/square/trine interpretations at lines 169-175, return-date labels, status/error messages, animation/graph labels, table search messages, share text 'Kopyalandı'). Needs a fork (/en/lilith-en.js) or a strings object. Specifics: keep the Turkish keys for parsing the backend; drop the decimal-comma .replace('.', ','); replace trT() with an English date format; replace trOfset() (Turkey UTC offset/DST, lines 64-73) with the browser's local offset or UTC; change the share URL. Good for i18n: interpretations in the result cards are read from the page DOM (burcMetni/evMetni/aciMetni, lines 85-88), so translating the HTML sections also translates most of the tool output. Anchor IDs (lilith-koc, lilith-ev-N, aci-gunes…) must match between the HTML and the SL/ACIK maps.

The EN page can drop the data-dg attributes and use native date/time inputs. That would need a small EN string table keyed on LANG; otherwise use a plain 'City, Country' text input.

turkey_specific_content: 1) lilith.js:64-73 trOfset() assumes Turkey time and Turkish DST history for every birth when no place is given (also used before server correction). Replace with the browser's local offset for that date (new Date(y,m-1,d,h,mi)) or UTC with a note. With a place, jdDuzelt() already corrects from the server's Moon position worldwide. Mean Lilith moves only 0.11° per day, so error stays tiny either way. 2) Ingress table note at line 456: 'Tarihler Türkiye saatine göre'. The 152-row table (1930-2040, line 455, data-b/data-s attributes) should be regenerated in UTC with the same ortalama() formula, with English date cells and sign names; this is scriptable, not hand translation. 3) Line 441: 'özellikle Türkiye'de 2016 öncesi yaz saati uygulaması' should become a generic note on daylight saving and historical time zones. 4) Placeholder 'Örn. İzmir' (line 382) should become 'e.g. London, UK'. 5) Turkish date formats ('27 Eylül 2026', trT) and decimal commas ('0,11 derece', '27,5 gün', JS .replace('.', ',')) should become English formats. 6) Turkish suffix arrays YE/DE (DE is unused) collapse to simple English. 7) JSON-LD: inLanguage tr-TR, priceCurrency TRY, operatingSystem 'Tüm tarayıcılar', breadcrumb 'Yıldız Günlüğü'; og:locale tr_TR; canonical and hreflang pairs are needed. 8) Date-bound section 'Şu an Lilith hangi burçta? 2026 ve 2027' (line 459) and the hard-coded initial 'Oğlak 1°' (line 381) need English rewrites (Capricorn 14 Sep 2026 – 11 Jun 2027, then Aquarius, then Pisces). 9) Related links (line 672) and the synastry link (line 617) point to Turkish pages; swap them for EN equivalents or remove them. 10) Membership autofill from the Turkish Supabase account (lilith.js:223) can be dropped. Otherwise the content is universal: astronomy of the lunar apogee, Mesopotamian/Adam myth, signs, houses, aspects. There are no Turkish culture, city, TL or e-Devlet references in the body text.

(b) .cta-kutu at line 662: 'Doğum Haritası Analizini incele →' to /dogum-haritasi-analizi.html, which is the paid ₺500 20+ page PDF report. (c) <!--AYBAG:oneri--> aside at line 671: Aşk Haritası ₺450 (/ask-haritasi-analizi.html), Karmik Harita ₺400 (/karmik-harita-analizi.html) and 'Tüm raporlar ve fiyatları →' /fiyatlar.html. (d) <!--AYBAG:ilgili--> links inside .ilgili at line 672 (ask-haritasi-analizi.html, karmik-harita-analizi.html). rationale:
I recommend this page for phase 1, as the flagship tool of the batch, but it is one of the costlier pages to translate and needs care in the JS.

Why it fits:
- The topic is universal and has strong English demand ("lilith sign", "black moon lilith calculator", "what is my lilith sign", plus a big long tail like "black moon lilith in scorpio" or "lilith in 8th house"), driven by the social-media Lilith trend.
- There is no Turkish cultural content apart from the timezone and DST code and one sentence.
- The tool is mostly client-side. Mean Lilith uses an analytic formula, true Lilith uses astronomy-engine, and return dates, the deviation graph and the orbit animation all run in the browser.
- The one backend call (/api/harita, used only for houses and aspects) returns Turkish, but the page uses only fixed vocabulary (sign/planet names and numbers), so a client dictionary is enough and no backend change is needed.
- Interpretations in the results are pulled from the page's own HTML sections, so translating the article also translates most of the tool output.
- It does more than most rival calculators: mean and true Lilith with degrees side by side, Placidus house, aspects with orbs, Lilith return dates, future transit-Lilith hits, a mean-vs-true deviation graph, and a searchable 1930-2040 ingress table.

What is hard:
- Translation is large. There are about 8,165 visible words: about 1,220 in the table (regenerate it by script, in UTC), about 3,500 in the 12 sign sections, about 1,200 in the 12 houses, and about 600 each in aspects and FAQ. The FAQ and HowTo JSON-LD repeat about 900 words.
- lilith.js has about 170 Turkish strings, about 60 of them prose. Only 1 Turkish string ('Hesabım') is truly inline in the HTML; the tool logic lives in the page-specific /lilith.js.
- Medium JS risk: Turkish sign and planet names are used as data keys for backend parsing (BN.indexOf(x.burc), N.p['Ay']). They must be kept internally, with separate display arrays.
- trOfset hard-codes Turkey time.
- dogum-giris.js and menu.js are Turkish.
- The backend quietly falls back to Ankara for places it can't find, and its Turkish 429 message carries a report upsell. The client must guard against both.

Competition is very high. Head terms are owned by astro-seek, cafeastrology, astrology.com, Astrostyle and lifestyle media (Allure, Cosmopolitan, Refinery29), plus many single-purpose Lilith-calculator sites. A brand-new /en/ section on a Turkish domain will struggle on 'lilith calculator' at first. The realistic wins are tool-specific long-tail queries where this page beats thin competitors: 'true vs mean lilith', 'lilith return calculator', 'black moon lilith house calculator', 'true lilith calculator'.

If phase 1 must stay low-effort, the article could ship trimmed. But the long-form sign and house sections both rank and feed the tool output, so cutting them weakens the page.
